name: Ruy López Steinitz Defense
summary: The Steinitz Defense (3...d6) solidly defends e5 with a rugged if cramped set-up championed by the first World Champion.
intro: The Steinitz Defense arises after 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 d6, meeting the pin on the c6-knight by directly propping up the e5-pawn. It is one of the oldest and soundest replies to the Ruy López, favouring solidity over activity: Black accepts a slightly cramped position in exchange for a structure that is difficult to break down. The move ...d6 does concede central space, and White typically strikes with d4 to increase the pressure, leaving Black to defend patiently and choose the right moment to release the central tension.
line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 d6

sections.heading: Strategic ideas
paragraphs: By playing 3...d6 Black shores up the e5-pawn at once, sidestepping the tactical tricks that surround the c6-knight and settling for a compact, low-risk formation. The cost is a measure of central space and a certain passivity: the queenside light-squared bishop is temporarily shut in behind its own pawn chain and usually needs the modest route ...Bd7 before it can breathe. Black's game is built on soundness and resilience rather than early activity, inviting White to overextend while the defence remains hard to crack.

White's natural response is to expand in the centre with d4, exploiting the extra space and increasing pressure against the e5-point. This confronts Black with a recurring strategic decision: whether to maintain the tension, release it with ...exd4, or allow White to resolve the centre. Yielding the centre too readily can leave Black cramped and passive for a long time, so accurate timing of the pawn exchanges, together with careful piece placement, is essential to keeping the defence sturdy rather than merely tenable.

sections.heading: Main variations
paragraphs: The critical line runs 4.d4, when White immediately challenges the centre. A well-known trap warns Black against passivity: after 4...Bd7 5.Nc3 the natural-looking developing moves are fine, but the careless 4...Bg4 or an ill-timed defence of e5 can walk into the tactical shot d4xe5 followed by Qa4 or Bxc6, exploiting the pin and the loosened defence. Sound handling usually involves ...Bd7, ...Nf6, ...Be7, and timely castling, after which Black defends a somewhat constricted but perfectly playable position.

In many lines White simply completes development with O-O, Nc3, and the central advance, aiming to convert the space advantage into lasting pressure. Black, for his part, must decide when to concede the centre with ...exd4 and how to activate the light-squared bishop, sometimes via ...Bd7-e8 or after a later ...g6. Because the Old Steinitz can become passive, modern practitioners more often prefer the Steinitz Deferred, inserting ...a6 first to gain the queenside options of the Morphy move order before committing to ...d6.

sections.heading: History and background
paragraphs: The defence is named after Wilhelm Steinitz, the first official World Champion, whose scientific school of positional play prized exactly this kind of rugged, structurally sound set-up. In the nineteenth century, when many masters chased sharp attacks, Steinitz championed the idea that a solid, defensible position could be held and gradually improved, and 3...d6 embodied that philosophy against the Spanish. His advocacy lent the line lasting theoretical respectability even as it acquired a reputation for being somewhat cramped.

As opening theory advanced, players came to feel that the immediate 3...d6 conceded too much space without adequate compensation, and the more flexible Steinitz Deferred, with ...a6 interpolated, largely superseded it at the top level. Nonetheless the Old Steinitz retains a following among those who value clarity and solidity, and it remains a sound, instructive choice, particularly useful for players learning how to hold a compact position against sustained pressure.
